final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package: 75% RVC with labor-value content, independent auditor verification, 60-day cure-and-tariff enforcement, and a six-year review mechanism (not hard sunset). Dairy separated into parallel bilateral track with identical enforcement teeth, both texts to capitals Friday. Canada accepted the framework conditional on locked enforcement language; Mexico signed on; Congress and industry demanded—and received—specific wage thresholds, auditor independence, and remedy sequences before committing.
minority_objections: Dairy agriculture initially demanded dairy access conditioned on auto package ratification, but was overruled by separate-track compromise
Supply-chain manufacturers repeatedly raised sunset/renewal uncertainty as investment-freeze trigger, but this was resolved late via review-mechanism commitment
key_conflicts: Canada's dairy supply-management red line vs. U.S. agriculture's demand for market access as ratification condition
Labor enforcement specificity: Congress/unions demanded breach definitions and remedy triggers, not framework promises
Auto industry's compliance-cost uncertainty vs. USTR's 75% RVC floor with no reopening
Timing pressure: Mexico and USTR pushed Friday lock-in; Canada and Congress demanded complete enforcement text first
key_concessions: Canada accepted 75% RVC and labor-value framework after securing binding enforcement annex with independent auditor
USTR separated dairy into parallel bilateral track (abandoning initial demand to condition trilateral on dairy)
Mexico accepted unilateral U.S. tariff authority in exchange for trilateral panel review step
USTR moved from hard six-year sunset to review mechanism to unlock business investment
Canada accepted dairy bilateral with identical 60-day enforcement structure as labor annex
red_lines: Canada: dairy supply management off the table unless U.S. offers equivalent concession (held throughout)
Congress/Labor: no ratification without enforceable labor breach definitions and tariff remedies (held, then satisfied)
Auto industry: no retooling commitment without locked compliance measurement and phase-in calendar (held, then satisfied)
USTR: 75% RVC floor non-negotiable, Mexico framework applies to Canada (held throughout)
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Dispute settlement (Chapter 19) never surfaced as Canadian concern despite historical importance
Steel/aluminum tariffs and Section 232 exemptions not discussed despite auto supply-chain relevance
Political ratification windows in Canada and Mexico beyond U.S. Congress timeline
Implementation capacity: who trains auditors, funds monitoring, enforces in practice
downstream_risk_variables: Dairy bilateral negotiation outcome and whether Canada's cabinet actually ratifies conditional on it
Congressional committee markup of enforcement language—whether Friday's text survives legislative process
Mexico's actual labor reform implementation vs. paper commitments
Auto industry capex decisions hinge on final auditor-certification language clarity
Review-mechanism design: does it create new uncertainty at six-year mark or provide genuine stability
uncertainty_notes: Sunset/review mechanism design details unresolved (auto-renew vs. opt-in). Dairy bilateral text not yet drafted—only framework agreed. Auditor appointment process and funding unclear. Notice-to-cure sequence (written notice before 60-day clock or day-one start) asked repeatedly but never explicitly answered by USTR in transcript. Wage-floor enforcement in practice (auditor capacity, data quality) assumed but not specified.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC and labor-value measurement drove the entire negotiation structure—Canada's entry conditional on enforcement annex, auto industry's retooling decisions gated on compliance clarity, multiple rounds spent defining auditor role and phase-in calendar. USTR's refusal to reopen RVC floor shaped all downstream concessions.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Congress and labor unions made ratification explicitly conditional on enforceable breach definitions, independent auditor verification, and tariff remedies—not framework promises. USTR's Friday draft commitment to wage thresholds ($16-$20), 60-day cure clock, and unilateral tariff authority was the decisive move that unlocked congressional and union support.
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy access was U.S. agriculture's stated ratification condition and Canada's explicit red line. The separate bilateral track with identical enforcement teeth was the compromise that allowed the trilateral package to proceed—dairy was the blocking issue until sequenced out.
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Never mentioned by Canada or any participant. Chapter 19 or state-to-state dispute mechanisms did not surface as a negotiation point.
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Supply-chain manufacturers explicitly stated hard sunset would trigger investment freeze and sourcing hedging. USTR's shift from six-year termination to review mechanism was the specific concession that unlocked business capex commitment and removed a ratification obstacle.
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress repeatedly conditioned support on seeing enforcement text (not promises), labor demanded breach definitions before voting, dairy agriculture tied ratification to market access, and auto industry gated retooling on compliance clarity. Ratification constraints shaped every major concession—USTR's Friday deadline, enforcement annex specificity, dairy bilateral structure.
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Raised multiple times as a concern (retooling cost, sourcing decisions, compliance uncertainty, capex freeze risk) but did not drive a specific proposal or concession. Industry asked for clarity and got it via enforcement annex and phase-in calendar, but the concern itself was acknowledged and addressed rather than being the forcing function.
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: Mexico and USTR explicitly used the bilateral framework as leverage—'Canada can join or negotiate separately,' 'we're not reopening the bilateral,' 'the political window closes.' Canada's acceptance of 75% RVC and labor framework was directly driven by the threat of being left outside a U.S.-Mexico deal. This was the structural pressure that forced Canada to negotiate within the existing terms rather than reopen them.
